outcome: No change to the McMullen problem (ν(d), the largest number such that any point set in general position in R^d admits a projective transformation into convex position) was found since 26 January 2024; the bounds 2d+1 ≤ ν(d) < 2d + ⌈(d+1)/2⌉ remain as established by Larman (1972) and Ramírez Alfonsín (2001), and the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1 remains open for d≥5.
summary: The triage flagged a possible AI connection because a November 2025 AlphaEvolve paper (Georgiev, Gómez-Serrano, Tao, Wagner, arXiv:2511.02864, 'Mathematical exploration and discovery at scale') tests AlphaEvolve on a list of 67 problems in analysis, combinatorics, geometry and number theory, and search summaries speculated the McMullen problem might be one of them. I resolved this directly: the paper's companion repository (github.com/google-deepmind/alphaevolve_repository_of_problems) numbers its 68 problem pages (67 problems plus one split into two logic-puzzle pages), and I fetched the title of every single one (problems/1.html through 68.html). None of them is the McMullen problem or any close variant. The list covers Kakeya/Nikodym sets, autocorrelation and Sidon-set problems, sphere/circle packing, kissing numbers, Sendov/Schmeisser/Borcea/Crouzeix conjectures, the Heilbronn problem, the Erdős–Szekeres Happy Ending problem, the moving sofa problem, and others — but nothing on projective transformations of point sets into convex position or on ν(d). The triage's speculation is therefore refuted, not confirmed. Separately, I found one genuinely relevant piece of scholarship in the window's neighborhood: 'On k-neighborly reorientations of oriented matroids' (Knauer et al., arXiv:2306.00414; published European Journal of Combinatorics 2024), whose abstract explicitly frames the k=1 case as 'the original statement' of McMullen's problem and generalizes to k≥2. I fetched the paper's HTML rendering and confirmed it proves no new result for k=1 (the actual McMullen problem as stated in our bullet) — for k=1 it only restates the existing bound from reference [6] (Ramírez Alfonsín 2001) — and its new bounds and computer-verified cases (ν(5,2), ν(6,2), ν(7,3), etc.) are all for k≥2, a different, changed question (k-neighborly polytopes rather than plain convex position). Under §3.1 this is a related/variant problem, not a case of the stated problem, so it does not count as progress here even though it is squarely about 'McMullen's problem' in the broader literature sense. Its v1 predates the frozen revision (June 2023) and its v2 (Feb 2024) is a minor revision shortly after; since the paper is out of scope regardless, the exact dating is moot. No source anywhere disclosed any AI/ML involvement in either the AlphaEvolve-repository check or the oriented-matroids paper (the latter mentions only 'by computer' exhaustive verification, i.e. classical computation, not an AI system). Wikipedia's own 'McMullen problem' and 'Convex position' articles both confirm the bounds are unchanged since 2001 and cite no post-2024 developments. I am satisfied this is a well-evidenced no-change case: the natural AI-related lead was checked exhaustively and closed out negative, and no non-AI progress on the exact stated problem surfaced either.
competing_reading: One could argue the k-neighborly reorientations paper 'is' progress on McMullen's problem in a loose sense, since the literature commonly calls the whole family (all k) 'McMullen's problem' or its generalizations, and the paper explicitly invokes McMullen's name. But our bullet's statement is specifically the k=1 convex-position question, and the paper leaves that exact case exactly where it was (citing the 2001 bound, no new result), so under the case-vs-variant test in §3.1 it is a variant (changing k) rather than a case (restricting the same question), and I classified it as out of scope.
what_would_settle_it: A paper or preprint stating a new bound on ν(d) itself (k=1) for some or all d, or a resolution of the conjecture ν(d)=2d+1 in any dimension d≥5, dated after 26 January 2024. Also, direct examination of the AlphaEvolve paper's full results tables (not just problem titles) would remove any residual doubt that a McMullen-adjacent problem was folded into one of the 68 listed under a different name — though the titles I retrieved (covering packing, autocorrelation, moving sofa, Erdős–Szekeres, etc.) leave essentially no ambiguity that convex position / projective transformation of point sets is simply not among them.
